# HTTP Errors and Deferred POST Decision Record

The early record tied default HTTP error mode too closely to empty deferred POST. After reviewing the client entry point, these should be kept as two separate topics: the former concerns what the default HTTP path passes to the caller; the latter concerns the success and failure behavior of a specific way of using POST. Both may involve "exceptions," but they do not support the same conclusion.

## Decision Retained at the Time

The default path continued to leave error responses to the caller. The proposal to convert all of them to transport exceptions was not adopted. The reason was the compatibility cost, not that empty deferred POST had passed validation. Existing callers Fang Ke can rely on the status code or content in the response; after a switch to exceptions, that information would no longer reach the caller in the same way.

This decision covers only the default HTTP error mode. It does not prescribe how callers must handle error responses, nor does it decide retries or the interpretation of response content on their behalf. The early draft used "empty POST looks abnormal" as a reason to change the handler. That inference is withdrawn.

## Leads from the Review

`Google_Client` in `src/Google/Client.php` is the starting point for this review. `LIBVER` and `USER_AGENT_SUFFIX` are near the class definition; `OAUTH2_REVOKE_URI`, `OAUTH2_TOKEN_URI`, `OAUTH2_AUTH_URL`, and `API_BASE_PATH` group the address and path bindings used by the client. `ApplicationDefaultCredentials`, `MemoryCacheItemPool`, `CredentialsLoader`, and `HttpHandlerFactory` at the top of the file are nearby dependencies for authentication and HTTP handling.

These objects point to continuing the investigation from the client entry point. They are not enough to establish either a success result or a failure result for empty deferred POST. The original statement that "an empty request will cause the default handler to throw an exception" is no longer retained; no sample call was attached at the time.

## Remaining Gaps

For empty deferred POST, the caller-visible results of successful and failed calls need to be recorded separately. If only one is obtained, the missing side should not be inferred from the default HTTP path. Keep the default-behavior decision in place for now, and continue investigating empty POST on its own.

# HTTP Errors and Deferred POST Decision Record

This record preserves a somewhat messy wrap-up process. The original issue title put the default HTTP error mode and empty deferred POST together, making it easy to read both as "the client throws an exception." It was only clarified later that there had not been enough samples for empty deferred POST at the time, while the default HTTP path already had its own compatibility tradeoff. The old issue title was not changed because people still use these two terms to get back here.

## Early comparison retained

The first version compared two approaches.

- The default handler converts HTTP errors into transport exceptions. This is more direct for callers concerned only with successful results, but changes legacy code that depends on the status code or response body.
- The default handler retains the error response, leaving it to the caller to decide whether to continue reading the response content or stop processing.

The second approach was chosen at the time to avoid having a single compatibility adjustment also change the callerFang Ke-visible error form. The wording then listed empty deferred POST as corroborating evidence for that tradeoff; that part was later overturned. Empty POST was merely a symptom that appeared at the same time and was still under investigation, insufficient to prove the default handler's behavior.

## Later review

The review of `src/Google/Client.php` reliably located `Google_Client` and the adjacent binding entries: `LIBVER`, `USER_AGENT_SUFFIX`, `OAUTH2_REVOKE_URI`, `OAUTH2_TOKEN_URI`, `OAUTH2_AUTH_URL`, and `API_BASE_PATH`. The file header also showed `ApplicationDefaultCredentials`, `MemoryCacheItemPool`, `CredentialsLoader`, and `HttpHandlerFactory`.

The correction made by this review concerns the record's scope; it does not treat adjacent names in the file as a complete request path. They were enough to lead the investigation back to the client entry point, but the successful and failed calls for empty deferred POST are still not attached here as a matched pair of results. The earlier claim that "an empty request alone could show that the handler would throw an exception" has been deprecated; it is retained to explain why the two issues were mistakenly combined at the time.

A passage once suggested changing the default handling for empty deferred POST first, then returning to confirm the caller impact. That ordering no longer applies: without observable results on both the success and failure sides, it is impossible to distinguish the behavior of the request itself from the choice made by the default HTTP path. Additional samples for empty POST should be collected separately later; it should no longer be used as a reason to change the default behavior.

## Current decision

> The default client HTTP handler sets http_errors to false so callers receive error responses instead of transport exceptions.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> DefaultHandler
    DefaultHandler --> ErrorResponse: http_errors = false
    ErrorResponse --> Caller
```

This fixes the form in which the default handler delivers error responses. A caller receiving a response does not mean it has handled that response correctly; the status code, response body, and whether to retry afterward are still determined by the caller's own logic. The old draft's alternative—"throwing exceptions uniformly might be simpler"—should no longer be treated as the current direction.

The existing history only calls for retaining the separately observable result of one successful call and one failed call. The available material does not provide the result contents, so they cannot be written here as any definite return value or exception type. If later samples show that this is related to the default HTTP path, a separate comparison should be made; until then, do not infer the default handler from the incomplete behavior observed with empty POST.

This page retains the old entry point and wording, so it can still be used to revisit the tradeoff from the compatibility issue. If more investigation is needed, start at the adjacency between `Google_Client` and `HttpHandlerFactory`; the two call results for empty POST remain the gap not filled here.

# Client alias interface adjustment proposal

This round of feedback corrected the framing in v1: the issue is not replacing the old class name in the file, but whether callers can continue to use it as a real compatibility entry point. Both the names and the OAuth v2 endpoint can be traced back starting from `src/Google/Client.php`, but the reasons for changing them differ. A name migration cannot substitute for an endpoint review.

In the file, `Google_Client` appears at the class declaration; the same section also retains `LIBVER` and `USER_AGENT_SUFFIX`. The OAuth addresses are grouped as `OAUTH2_REVOKE_URI`, `OAUTH2_TOKEN_URI`, and `OAUTH2_AUTH_URL`, with `API_BASE_PATH` as well. We previously treated these constants as evidence that "the endpoints are unified," but later withdrew that claim: having the constants in one place only confirms public reference points, not that every authentication path gets its value from the same address.

The naming options are now compared by cost to callers, not by whether the class name is old or new.

| Option | What is retained | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Keep both names | Callers can use both the legacy name and the namespaced name | Both loading and construction paths require ongoing verification |
| Keep only migration guidance | New integrations use only the namespaced name | Existing callers must handle the name difference themselves |
| Remove the legacy name | Only one name remains | Compatibility risk is passed directly to existing integrations |

The third option is out of scope for this round. The second was not adopted as the default path in review either: it turns failures for existing callers into a migration-documentation issue without answering whether the old entry point is actually still usable. Authentication dependencies near the client, such as `Google\Auth\CredentialsLoader` and `Google\Auth\HttpHandler\HttpHandlerFactory`, are only starting points for inspecting the authentication boundary; they do not determine whether the alias works.

The requirement is now stated as verifiable interface semantics rather than migration advice: The modern Google\Client and legacy Google_Client classes are both autoloadable and instantiable; the legacy_alias remains a concrete compatibility name.

This requirement separates three judgments that were previously conflated. Autoloadable means the name can be loaded; instantiable means an object can be constructed after loading; `legacy_alias` is not merely a historical string for searches or hints. If any of these fails, the dual-name option has not met its compatibility goal. "The modern name works" cannot stand in for that result.

The OAuth v2 endpoint remains narrowly scoped. The client constants are the first place to check, but regression results must be retained separately for the authorization, token, and revocation addresses. Do not infer that the other two work just because one is read correctly. This also makes no commitment to changing authentication dependencies or caching logic. The presence of authentication dependencies only explains why endpoint review needs to examine code adjacent to the client; it cannot substitute for user-visible address behavior.

The trial has the following stop conditions: if the legacy name works only with a particular loading order, stop treating it as a stable compatibility name; if the namespaced name works but the legacy name cannot be instantiated, retain the observed failure and return to name loading; if an endpoint issue can only be bypassed by callers overriding the address themselves, stop claiming that the client constants have consolidated address handling. Conversely, even when all three addresses pass their respective user-visible regressions, that does not automatically establish that name compatibility is complete.

It is still undecided which name the examples for new integrations should show first. That choice does not affect the dual-name requirement, but it will affect the default wording of later migration material. The next review will add only this decision and the regression records for the three endpoint types, without expanding into other authentication configuration options.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Cache Identity and Authentication Options

Initially, the incident was split into two adjacent threads: whether the cache object handed by the caller to the client could still be found later, and where auth client options entered the authentication call. Neither thread had a complete construction snippet at the time, so they could not explain each other.

Record the entry point first at `src/Google/Client.php`. The `Google_Client` in the file is the starting point for tracing back to the client-construction call; near the top of the file are the names for authentication, caching, and HTTP handling:

```php
use Google\Auth\ApplicationDefaultCredentials;
use Google\Auth\Cache\MemoryCacheItemPool;
use Google\Auth\CredentialsLoader;
use Google\Auth\HttpHandler\HttpHandlerFactory;
```

The same file also contains `OAUTH2_AUTH_URL`, `OAUTH2_TOKEN_URI`, and `OAUTH2_REVOKE_URI`. These names help locate code near the client, but cannot substitute for an actual call context. Seeing the OAuth endpoint does not mean the caller supplied authentication options; seeing `MemoryCacheItemPool` also does not mean a given call used the default cache.

Keep two points on the cache path: the cache object actually received during construction, and the return value obtained from `getCache()`() on the same client. Cache keys, entry contents, hit/miss status, and the return value's class name are not the object itself. If the original object is absent at the construction site, or the return value was not saved, record a gap; do not infer that the object was replaced from "the cache did not hit."

```text
Cache description appears
├─ Cannot find Google_Client construction call: return to the caller
├─ Found the call but no visible cache object: record no injection or an unconfirmed state
└─ Constructor argument is present
   ├─ No getCache() return value: pause identity assessment
   └─ Both are present: retain the comparison context
```

On the authentication path, keep the option-creation site and the order in which the options enter the client call separate. If the only known fact is that "an exception appeared when options were supplied," write it first as a co-occurring observation; without a comparable call that omitted the options, do not write it as a necessary condition. The option contents, default values, and override order do not appear in the evidence; do not fill them in from the names `CredentialsLoader` or `HttpHandlerFactory`.

An early hypothesis was that the default cache path might explain why the external object no longer appeared. This hypothesis lacks the constructor argument and returned object, so retain it only as a direction for further investigation.

# Cache Identity and Authentication Options Troubleshooting Tree

The first version put "the cache is wrong" and "the auth client has options" on the same page because both descriptions came from the same kind of client incident. On review, putting them side by side does not establish causation. For cache identity, look only at the constructor input and the `getCache()` return value; for authentication options, look only at where they were created, the order in which they were passed, and whether a comparison call exists.

## Where to Start Checking

Continue using `src/Google/Client.php` to locate `Google_Client`. The file contains `LIBVER`, `USER_AGENT_SUFFIX`, `API_BASE_PATH`, and three OAuth URI constants; the file header also imports `ApplicationDefaultCredentials`, `MemoryCacheItemPool`, `CredentialsLoader`, and `HttpHandlerFactory`. This shows that the client file sits alongside both authentication and cache code, but does not show which path a particular runtime call took.

An earlier shorthand note linked the OAuth name directly to the default cache:

```text
Authentication-related name found
  -> Check the OAuth endpoint
  -> Check the default in-memory cache
  -> Cache miss
  -> The external cache may no longer be in use
```

This note is retained here to help identify the source of older reports, but it is no longer the investigation sequence. Endpoint constants are static declarations, the default pool is only a candidate for calls without injection, and a miss is an observation from a single read. Without the construction details and an object comparison connecting them, these cannot be written up directly as a change in cache object.

## Cache Branch

First, find the call that creates `Google_Client`. Once found, confirm exactly which object was passed into construction. The caller may have an outer wrapper, or may perform a conversion before construction; the first variable encountered is not necessarily the actual argument. On the other side, obtain the raw `getCache()` return value as well, rather than substituting a variable that wraps it after retrieval.

The comparison must use the same client instance:

```text
Are both the constructor argument and the getCache() return value available?
├─ No: State whether the original object or return value is missing, and stop the identity branch
└─ Yes
   ├─ The comparison is against a wrapper: Go back to the constructor argument and raw return value
   └─ Both sides can be compared directly: Record the result
      ├─ They appear to match: Investigate entries and timing of use separately
      └─ They appear to differ: First check for conversion, wrapping, or client recreation
```

The following records cannot replace the comparison:

- Matching cache keys only indicate that the naming may be similar; they do not retain object references.
- Matching entry contents may come from different objects; different contents may simply reflect different read times.
- A return value of the same class as the expected object only indicates similar types.
- A single miss does not, by itself, show that the client recreated the cache.
- The presence of `MemoryCacheItemPool` in the file header cannot override a constructor argument already observed.

Keep calls without an injected object separate from calls where an object was supplied. For the former, continue looking for the default path; for the latter, preserve the input and return value first. If it is not even clear whether an object was injected in the incident, stop at "construction unconfirmed" rather than treating the default path as counterevidence.

## Authentication Options Branch

Records of auth client options should first answer two questions: where the options were created, and whether they entered the call before or after client creation. If the options came from another client or an outer configuration object, retain that point of transfer as well. When the material does not provide the complete configuration, do not fill in key names, default rules, or precedence.

When comparable calls with and without options are available, record whether the abnormal behavior occurs only in the former; when there is only one incident, write "options were present in the incident." This provides a comparison lead, not a substitute for establishing the relationship between cache objects.

```text
Authentication abnormality occurs
├─ Options creation site not located: Record the gap; do not fill in configuration details
└─ Creation site found
   ├─ No comparison call without options: The condition is not yet established
   └─ Comparison available: Record whether the abnormality occurs only in calls with options
```

When cache objects and authentication options are present in the same incident, the two branches can be recorded in parallel, but do not merge their conclusions. Finding where the options were created still cannot replace the two sides of the cache comparison; cache objects that appear similar do not also prove that the options were passed correctly.

## Review Addendum

The first version's claim that "the default cache may take over from the external object" remains a working hypothesis. It lacks the actual constructor argument and a return value from the same client. Follow-up incidents should prioritize filling these two gaps, rather than continuing to infer from OAuth URL or class names. If the object comparison is complete but entries are still abnormal, move the investigation to entry reads and writes and the timing of use; do not keep using the identity branch to explain every cache symptom.

# Cache Identity and Authentication Options Troubleshooting Tree

This page was originally an entry point for two descriptions that were easy to conflate: injected cache identity and auth client options. They often appeared together in client issues, so early troubleshooting would jump from the authentication name to the cache name and then mistake a single miss for an object change. Later additions did not remove those old passages because some incidents still left only the same terse clues: an OAuth address, a cache class name, or the statement "the passed-in cache did not come back."

When opening this page now, first check whether the report actually contains a construction call, the actual cache object, and the `getCache()` return value. If those locations are absent, the appropriate action is to locate the next section of code, not to fill in a cause for the incident. The same applies to the authentication path: seeing option names does not mean that the creation site has been found, much less that the cache object can be explained.

## 2023-05-24: Initial Entry Record

The initial record only established that the issue was somewhere near the client; it did not include a complete call fragment. It did not show where the cache object was passed to the client or where it was retrieved after the call. The authentication options were only mentioned, so it could not be confirmed whether they were prepared before client construction, added afterward, or passed from another object.

At the time, the entry was recorded at `src/Google/Client.php`. In the file, `Google_Client` can be located, along with the following direct dependency:

```php
use Google\Auth\ApplicationDefaultCredentials;
use Google\Auth\Cache\MemoryCacheItemPool;
use Google\Auth\CredentialsLoader;
use Google\Auth\HttpHandler\HttpHandlerFactory;
```

The same file also contains the endpoint constants `LIBVER`, `USER_AGENT_SUFFIX`, `API_BASE_PATH`, and OAuth. The initial notes treated these names as signposts for further reading: `OAUTH2_AUTH_URL`, `OAUTH2_TOKEN_URI`, and `OAUTH2_REVOKE_URI` could lead to authentication-related locations; `MemoryCacheItemPool` could indicate that a default cache path might exist. At the time, they were not treated as runtime evidence, only as static adjacency visible in this area.

The first-pass procedure sketch was brief:

```text
First find Google_Client
├─ Find a construction call: copy down the constructor arguments
└─ Cannot find a construction call: continue from the caller
```

The sketch did not make clear that the "constructor arguments" and the caller's variables might not be at the same level, nor did it state that the return value of `getCache()` should be obtained from the same client instance. At the time, the focus was simply to avoid treating a cache key or a single hit result as the input object.

The initial hypothesis held that, when the external cache no longer appeared, the default cache path was worth checking. This was only a candidate at the time: there was no actual constructor argument and no returned object. Auth options were noted alongside it, because they appeared in similar reports, not because we had already seen them affect the cache.

## 2023-05-25: Review margin notes

The first sentence added during review was: "Preserve the passed-in object first, then discuss the default path." This changed the troubleshooting priority. The `MemoryCacheItemPool` in the file header can only help identify candidates for calls without injection; once the call site already has an actual constructor argument, the default pool name should not be used to infer that the argument was replaced.

The second margin note was: "Keep the creation site separate for the auth path." The reason is straightforward: OAuth URI appear in the client file, which only shows that the client has an endpoint entry point. It cannot show that the caller ever passed auth client options, nor that those options are related to the cache.

After the review, the call-site data to retain was divided into two groups:

```text
Cache: the object actually received during construction; the return value of the same client's getCache()
Auth: where the options are created; the order in which they reach the client call; whether a comparison call exists
```

Here, "actually received" requires particular caution. A call to Fang Ke may first hold a wrapper object, then extract the internal object and pass it to the client; it may also convert first and then construct. Even if an outer variable is named like a cache, it may not be the left-hand operand needed for the comparison. The other side may also be wrapped again by the caller after `getCache()`, so the wrapped variable cannot replace the original return value.

This margin note did not provide the keys, default values, or override order of the auth options.`CredentialsLoader`,`ApplicationDefaultCredentials` and `HttpHandlerFactory` are still only places to continue reading in the file. Without a call site, these names cannot be used to infer specific configuration.

## 2023-08-21: A counterexample left by one recheck

The description encountered during rechecking was"Auth client options exist, but the cache was not hit." That record preserved neither the constructor argument nor the `getCache()` return value. The old sticky note had written it as"Auth settings may recreate the cache." This assessment remains in its original location, but can no longer be used.

It contains at least two observations: authentication-related options were mentioned; a cache read did not meet expectations. It does not include both objects, so it cannot answer whether the client holds the original object, much less show that the authentication options changed the object. When similar descriptions come up again, split them into two gaps: whether the place where the authentication options were created can be found; whether the cache input and return value can be retained on the same client.

There was also a weaker attempt in the same round: comparing only the class name of the return value. The return value was still treated as a cache class, so the notes said, "It should still be the original cache." This conclusion is also invalid. Identical class names can only indicate similar types, not that they are the same instance; different class names also cannot independently show that the client replaced the object, unless it is already clear that the comparison is between the constructor argument and the original return value.

Cache keys, entry contents, and hit status have the same problem. Two different objects may read the same entry, making it look as though "the cache is still there"; the same object may also produce a miss because of differences in read timing or entry state, making it look as though "the cache has changed." These observations are worth retaining, but they are clues about entries or timing of use and cannot be reduced to identity judgments.

The branches added at the time were as follows:

```text
Are both the constructor argument and the return value of getCache() available?
├─ No: state which side is missing; pause the identity judgment
└─ Yes
   ├─ The left side is only a surrounding wrapper: keep looking for the value passed into the construction process
   ├─ The right side is only an outer wrapper: retain the original getCache() return value
   └─ Both sides can be compared directly: record the result, then decide the next step
```

This review did not require every cache issue to start with the identity branch. If a report only describes abnormal entry reads or writes, without saying that "the passed-in object no longer appears," entries or timing of use can be checked first. Only when the report actually points to the relationship between the construction input and the returned object should this comparison path be used.

## 2023-08-22: The retained old shortcut

After review, an early shorthand note was marked as deprecated, with its original text retained:

```text
See the OAuth endpoint constant
  -> Check the default in-memory cache
  -> See a cache miss
  -> Conclude that the external cache was not used
```

The problem with this path is not that the endpoint constant or the default cache name does not exist. The problem is that it skips the call site. OAuth URI is a fixed entry point in the client file; the default pool is a candidate for further inspection when no object has been injected; a miss is the result of one read. Even linked together, these three still cannot answer whether an external object was provided during construction, nor what object was subsequently retrieved.

There was also an even shorter old line of reasoning from the same period: "As soon as authentication client options appear, first suspect that they override the cache." It came from a direction of investigation, not a confirmed observation. Without the place where the options were created, the order in which they were passed, the constructor arguments, or the returned object, this statement can only be retained as a hypothesis awaiting evidence.

The old path is easy to reuse because the OAuth constant and the cache import are both adjacent to `Google_Client`. Their static proximity reads like a runtime relationship. When investigating, first ask "Which section of code does this name lead me to?" and then ask "Is there evidence of the corresponding action in this case?" If the second question has no answer, stop at navigation; do not write it up as attribution.

## Old example: only the default pool name is visible

This example has not been removed from the page. In the past, people saw `MemoryCacheItemPool` and treated it as the default answer for every cache case. It now retains only one narrow use: when a constructor call has no visible cache object, it can suggest continuing to look for the default path.

If the constructor call explicitly includes an object, the default pool name is not counterevidence that the object was replaced. If it is not even clear whether the constructor call includes an object, "there is a default pool import at the top of the file" must not be written as "there was no injection at runtime" either. This old example exists to help readers recognize skipped steps in old reports, not to provide a current conclusion.

## Old example: only the OAuth address is visible

Another old-style record inferred from the appearance of `OAUTH2_TOKEN_URI` in the client file that "the authentication client options have taken effect." That inference was later crossed out. The endpoint can help locate the OAuth code, but it cannot prove what options the caller supplied or which client instance those options entered.

Likewise, the presence of `OAUTH2_AUTH_URL` and `OAUTH2_REVOKE_URI` does not indicate that the authentication call went through any particular configuration. If the only evidence in the case is an endpoint or class name, write "creation site not located" for the authentication branch, then return to the caller to look for the actions that prepare and pass the configuration. Without those actions, do not fill in option contents or treat URI as a configuration record.

## 2024-11-15: investigation order starting from symptoms

The current sequence starts with observable symptoms, not the most familiar static names. Both symptoms can appear in the same case, but each line of investigation has its own stopping conditions.

### The passed-in cache does not appear further along

First, find the call that creates `Google_Client`. If it cannot be found, record that the constructor entry point is missing and return to the caller; do not infer runtime behavior from the import of `src/Google/Client.php`.

After finding the constructor call, confirm whether the construction process actually received a cache object. If there is no object, record that there was no injection or that it has not yet been confirmed. You can continue looking for the default path here, but do not include this case in an object identity comparison. If an object is present, save the actual argument that entered the construction process, not just the outer wrapper, cache key, or an earlier substitute variable.

Then obtain `getCache()` from the same client instance. If no return value can be obtained, note that the return value is missing and stop the identity check. If a return value can be obtained, first confirm that the value retained is the original return value, not a subsequent wrapper added by the caller, then compare the two sides.

```text
Cache description appears
|
+-- Found the Google_Client constructor call?
|   |
|   +-- No: construction entry point missing, return to the caller
|   |
|   +-- Yes
|       |
|       +-- Is there an actual cache object during construction?
|       |   |
|       |   +-- No: record no injection or unconfirmed; check the default path separately if needed
|       |   |
|       |   +-- Yes
|       |       |
|       |       +-- Can getCache() be obtained from the same client?
|       |           |
|       |           +-- No: return value missing, stop the identity check
|       |           |
|       |           +-- Yes: compare the actual argument with the original return value
|       |               ├─ Match: move on to checking entries or the time of use
|       |               └─ Mismatch: check for wrapping, conversion, or client recreation
```

If the comparison shows a match, the identity branch ends. Cache misses, entry contents that do not meet expectations, and subsequent wrapping of the return value should each be investigated further in their respective contexts. If the comparison shows a mismatch, first look in the caller for conversion before construction, object wrapping, or client recreation; if none of these actions are observed, record only that the two sides differ and that the cause is still undetermined.

The stopping point here is not "we still do not know why there was no cache hit." The stopping point is that the object comparison has not been completed. Entry issues can still be investigated, and authentication issues can still be investigated, but the report must not turn the gap left by missing objects on the two sides into "the client replaced the cache."

### An exception occurs when auth client options are present

For the authentication investigation, first determine whether there is an actual comparison. If comparable calls both with and without options are available, record whether the exception occurs only in calls with options. If there is only a single observed case, record "the options are present in this case," and do not elevate this to a necessary condition.

Next, find where the options are created and the order in which they are passed: are they prepared before client creation, passed into the call only after creation, or supplied by an adjacent object? If the creation site cannot be found, write "creation site not located." Do not infer option keys, default rules, or override order from OAuth URI, `CredentialsLoader`, `ApplicationDefaultCredentials`, or `HttpHandlerFactory` just to fill out the record.

```text
Authentication exception occurs
|
+-- Can the option creation site be located?
|   |
|   +-- No: Record that the creation site has not been located; do not fill in configuration details
|   |
|   +-- Yes: Record the creation site and its order relative to entry into the client call
|
+-- Is there a control call without the options?
    |
    +-- No: Only one observed case; the conditions have not yet been confirmed
    |
    +-- Yes: Preserve whether the exception occurs only in calls with the options
```

The authentication and cache investigation tracks should retain evidence in parallel. Locating where the authentication options are created does not replace comparing the cache objects; completing the cache object comparison also does not prove that the authentication options are passed correctly or will not affect other authentication behavior. Include the caller's conversion, reconstruction, or passing actions in the cause description only if those actions have actually been observed in the case.

## Current requirement

For a client supplied with a cache object at construction time, the current assessment is based on object identity: A cache object supplied through the client constructor is retained by identity and getCache() returns that same object as cache_identity.

This requirement covers only the cache object supplied through client construction and the `getCache()` result obtained from that same client. It does not address cache entry hits, the source of the default cache, the OAuth endpoint, or the effects of auth client options on other authentication behavior.

The operational record should preserve the following in the order they occurred: whether the `Google_Client` constructor call was found; whether there was an actual cache argument; whether the left-hand side was the object that actually entered the construction process; whether the original `getCache()` return value was obtained from the same client; and what was observed after comparing the two sides. For authentication, add only the option creation site, its order relative to entry into the call, and whether a control exists. This allows the next review to return to specific objects rather than guessing again from names or cache misses.

## Issues still not disentangled

The actual scope of auth client options has not been fully documented here. If the investigation continues, preserve where the options are prepared, the order in which they enter `Google_Client`, and whether there is a control call without those options. Without this information, the authentication track cannot provide a causal explanation for the cache track.

The wrapper layer is another adjacent boundary that has not been disentangled. The caller Fang Ke may save only the outer object before it is passed in, or may save only the outer object after `getCache()`. The former lacks the constructor argument, and the latter lacks the original return value; identical class names, identical keys, or identical entry contents cannot fill either of these gaps.

## Appendix: How to translate old reports

"Cache miss" should be translated as an entry or an observation at the point of use, unless both ends of the object have already been compared. It can lead to read/write order and entry state, but it cannot automatically enter the identity-change branch.

"Returned value is also a cache class" is merely a type record. Without constructor arguments and the original `getCache()` return value, it cannot be treated as a conclusion about the object relationship.

"Default cache exists" should be kept separate from "whether this call injects an object." The default pool can be used to continue checking calls with no visible arguments; when constructor input already exists, do not use the default path to negate the input.

"Authentication option is used" requires seeing at least where it is created or passed. If all we see are `OAUTH2_AUTH_URL`, `OAUTH2_TOKEN_URI`, or `OAUTH2_REVOKE_URI`, the record can say at most that the client file provides a OAuth entry.

# Troubleshooting Tree for Cache Identity and Authentication Options

This page was originally created as an entry point for two descriptions that are easily conflated: injected cache identity, and auth client options. They often appear together in client issues, so early troubleshooting would jump from authentication names to cache names, then treat a cache miss as a change in the object. Later additions did not remove those older passages, because some cases still leave only similarly brief clues: a OAuth address, a cache class name, or a statement that "the cache passed in did not come back".

When opening this page now, first check whether the report actually includes a constructor call, the actual cache object, and the return value of `getCache()`. If these are missing, the next step is to locate the next section of code, not to fill in a cause for the reported case. The same applies to the authentication branch: seeing a mention of options does not mean their creation site has been found, much less that the cache object can be explained.

## 2023-05-24: Initial Entry-Point Notes

The initial record only established that the issue was somewhere around the client; it did not include a complete call snippet. There was no record of where the cache object was passed to the client or where it was retrieved after the call. Authentication options were also only mentioned, so it was impossible to confirm whether they were prepared before client construction, attached after construction, or passed from another object.

At the time, `src/Google/Client.php` was recorded as the entry point. The file contains `Google_Client`, and the following direct dependencies are visible:

```php
use Google\Auth\ApplicationDefaultCredentials;
use Google\Auth\Cache\MemoryCacheItemPool;
use Google\Auth\CredentialsLoader;
use Google\Auth\HttpHandler\HttpHandlerFactory;
```

The same file also contains the endpoint constants `LIBVER`, `USER_AGENT_SUFFIX`, `API_BASE_PATH`, and OAuth. The initial notes treated these names as signposts for further reading: `OAUTH2_AUTH_URL`, `OAUTH2_TOKEN_URI`, and `OAUTH2_REVOKE_URI` could lead to authentication-related locations; `MemoryCacheItemPool` could suggest that a default cache path might exist. They were not treated as runtime evidence at the time, only as visible static relationships in this area.

The first-pass procedure sketch was brief:

```text
First locate Google_Client
├─ Constructor call found: copy the constructor arguments
└─ Constructor call not found: continue looking from the caller
```

The sketch did not clarify that "constructor arguments" and the caller's variables might be at different levels, nor did it state that the return value of `getCache()` should be obtained from the same client instance. The focus at the time was simply to avoid treating a cache key or the result of a single cache hit as the input object.

The initial hypothesis was that when the external cache no longer appeared, the default cache path was worth checking. At the time, this was only a candidate explanation: there were no constructor arguments and no returned object. The authentication options were noted alongside it because they appeared in similar reports, not because they had already been observed affecting the cache.

## 2023-05-25: Review margin notes

The first sentence added during review was: "First preserve the object passed in, then discuss the default path." This changed the investigation priorities. The `MemoryCacheItemPool` at the top of the file can only help identify candidate calls without injection; once constructor arguments are available at the call site, the default pool name should not be used to infer that an argument was replaced.

The second margin note was: "For the authentication track, record the creation site separately." The reason is straightforward: the presence of OAuth URI in the client file only indicates that the client has an endpoint entry point. It does not show that the caller passed in auth client options, nor does it show that those options have anything to do with the cache.

After the review, the call-site evidence was split into two groups of data to retain:

```text
Cache: the object actually received during construction; the return value of getCache() on the same client
Authentication: where the options were created; the order in which they entered client calls; whether there was a comparison call
```

"Actually received" needs to be treated especially cautiously here. The caller Fang Ke may first hold a wrapper object, then extract the internal object and pass it to the client; it may also perform a conversion before construction. Even if an outer variable has a cache-like name, it is not necessarily the left-hand side needed for the comparison. The other side may also be wrapped again by the caller after `getCache()`, so the wrapped variable cannot substitute for the original return value.

These margin notes did not provide the authentication option keys, default values, or override order. `CredentialsLoader`, `ApplicationDefaultCredentials`, and `HttpHandlerFactory` are still only places to continue reading within the file. Without evidence from the call site, no specific configuration can be inferred from these names.

## 2023-08-21: A counterexample left by a recheck

The description encountered during the recheck was "Authentication client options are present, but there was no cache hit." That record preserved neither the constructor arguments nor the return value of `getCache()`. An old note had described it as "Authentication settings may recreate the cache." That assessment remains in its original location, but can no longer be relied on.

It contains at least two observations: authentication-related options were mentioned; a cache read did not meet expectations. It does not include both objects, so it cannot answer whether the client holds the original object, much less show that the authentication options changed the object. When similar descriptions come up later, split them into two gaps: whether the place where the authentication options were created can be found; whether the cache input and return value can be retained on the same client.

There was also a weaker attempt in the same round: comparing only the class name of the return value. The return value was still considered to be a cache class, so the note said, "It should still be the original cache." This conclusion is also invalid. The same class name only indicates similar types, not that they are the same instance; different class names also cannot independently show that the client replaced the object, unless it is already clear that the comparison is between the constructor argument and the original return value.

Cache keys, entry contents, and hit status have the same problem. Two different objects may read the same entry, making it look as though "the cache is still there"; the same object may also produce a miss because of differences in read timing or entry state, making it look as though "the cache has changed." These observations are worth retaining, but they are clues about entries or timing of use and cannot be reduced to an identity judgment.

The branches added at the time were as follows:

```text
Are both the constructor argument and the getCache() return value available?
├─ No: state which side is missing; pause the identity judgment
└─ Yes
   ├─ The left side is only a surrounding wrapper: keep looking for the value that enters the construction process
   ├─ The right side is only an outer wrapper: retain the original getCache() return value
   └─ Both sides can be compared directly: record the result, then decide the next step
```

This review did not require every cache issue to start with the identity branch. If a report only describes abnormal entry reads or writes and does not say that "the passed-in object no longer appears," entries or timing of use can be checked first. Enter this comparison path only when the report actually points to the relationship between the constructor input and the returned object.

## 2023-08-22: The retained old shortcut path

After review, an early shorthand note was marked as deprecated, with the original text retained:

```text
See the OAuth endpoint constant
  -> Check the default in-memory cache
  -> See a cache miss
  -> Conclude that the external cache was not used
```

The problem with this path is not that the endpoint constant or default cache name does not exist. The problem is that it skips the call site. OAuth URI is a fixed entry point in the client file; the default pool is a candidate that can be checked further when no object is injected; a miss is the result of a single read. Even when linked together, these three still cannot answer whether an external object was provided during construction, or what object was subsequently obtained.

There was also an even shorter old formulation from the same period: "As soon as authentication client options appear, first suspect that they override the cache." It came from a direction of investigation, not a confirmed observation. Without the place where the options were created, the passing order, the constructor argument, or the returned object, this statement can only be retained as a hypothesis awaiting verification.

The old path is easy to reuse because the OAuth constant and the cache import are both near `Google_Client`. Their static locations are close together, making them look like a runtime relationship. When troubleshooting, first ask "Which section of code does this name lead me to?", then ask "Does the evidence from this case show the corresponding action?" If the second question has no answer, stop at navigation; do not write it up as an attribution.

## Old example: Only the default pool name is visible

This example has not been removed from the page. In the past, some people saw `MemoryCacheItemPool` and treated it as the default answer for every cache-related case. It now retains only one narrow use: when no cache object is visible in the constructor call, it can suggest continuing to look for the default path.

If the constructor call clearly includes an object, the default pool name is not evidence against that object having been replaced. If it is not even clear whether the constructor call includes an object, "there is a default pool import at the top of the file" cannot be written as "there was no injection at runtime". This old example exists to help readers recognize skipped steps in old reports, not to provide a current conclusion.

## Old example: Only the OAuth address is visible

Another old-style record went from `OAUTH2_TOKEN_URI` appearing in the client file to "the authentication client options have taken effect". That inference was later crossed out. The endpoint can help locate the OAuth code, but it cannot prove what options the caller supplied or which client instance received them.

Likewise, the presence of `OAUTH2_AUTH_URL` and `OAUTH2_REVOKE_URI` does not show that the authentication call went through a particular configuration. If the evidence from the case contains only an endpoint or class name, write "creation site not located" in the authentication branch, then return to the caller to look for the actions that prepare and pass the configuration. Without these actions, do not fill in the option contents or treat URI as a configuration record.

## 2024-11-15: Troubleshooting sequence starting from symptoms

The current sequence starts with observable symptoms, rather than the most familiar static names. The two symptoms can appear in the same case, but each line of investigation has its own stopping conditions.

### The passed-in cache does not appear further along

First, find the call that creates `Google_Client`. If you cannot find it, record that the construction entry point is missing and return to the caller; do not infer runtime behavior from the `src/Google/Client.php` import.

After finding the constructor call, confirm whether the construction process actually received a cache object. If there is no object, record no injection or not yet confirmed. You can continue looking for the default path here, but do not include this case in an object identity comparison. If an object is present, save the actual argument that entered the construction process, not just an outer wrapper, cache key, or earlier substitute variable.

Then obtain `getCache()` from the same client instance. If the return value cannot be obtained, state that the return value is missing and stop determining the identity. If the return value is obtained, first confirm that the value retained is the original return value, not a subsequent wrapper added by the caller, and then compare the two sides.

```text
Cache description appears
|
+-- Found a Google_Client construction call?
|   |
|   +-- No: construction entry point is missing; return to the caller
|   |
|   +-- Yes
|       |
|       +-- Does the construction process have an actual cache object?
|       |   |
|       |   +-- No: record no injection or unconfirmed; check the default path separately if needed
|       |   |
|       |   +-- Yes
|       |       |
|       |       +-- Can the same client obtain getCache()?
|       |           |
|       |           +-- No: return value is missing; stop determining the identity
|       |           |
|       |           +-- Yes: compare the actual arguments with the original return value
|       |               ├─ Consistent: investigate the entry or the point of use
|       |               └─ Inconsistent: investigate wrapping, conversion, or client reconstruction
```

When the comparison is consistent, this identity branch ends. A cache miss, unexpected entry contents, or a return value subsequently wrapped should each be investigated further in its respective context. When the comparison is inconsistent, first look in the caller for conversion before construction, object wrapping, or an action that recreates the client; when none of these actions are visible, only record that the two sides differ—the cause remains undetermined.

The stopping point here is not "we still do not know why there was no cache hit." The stopping point is that the object comparison was not completed. Entry issues can continue to be investigated, and authentication issues can also continue to be investigated, but the report must not turn the absence of objects on both sides into "the client replaced the cache."

### An exception occurs with auth client options

The authentication track should first determine whether there is a genuine comparison. If there are comparable calls both with and without options, record whether the exception occurs only in the call with options. If there is only a single case, record "options appear with the case"; do not elevate this to a necessary condition.

Next, find where the options are created and the order in which they are passed: are they prepared before the client is created, do they enter the call only after creation, or are they provided by an adjacent object? If the creation site cannot be found, write "creation site not located." Do not infer option keys, default rules, or override order from OAuth URI, `CredentialsLoader`, `ApplicationDefaultCredentials` or `HttpHandlerFactory` merely to fill out the record.

```text
Authentication exception occurs
|
+-- Can the options creation site be located?
|   |
|   +-- No: record that the creation site has not been located; do not add configuration details
|   |
|   +-- Yes: record the creation site and its order relative to entry into the client call
|
+-- Is there a comparison call without the options?
    |
    +-- No: only one observed case; the conditions have not yet been confirmed
    |
    +-- Yes: record whether the exception occurs only in calls with the options
```

The authentication and cache investigation tracks should be documented in parallel. Locating where the authentication options are created does not replace comparing the cache objects; completing the cache object comparison also does not prove that the authentication options are passed correctly or that they will not affect other authentication behavior. Include the caller's conversion, reconstruction, or passing actions in the explanation of the cause only if those actions have already been observed in the case.

## Current requirement

For a client supplied with a cache object during construction, the current assessment is based on object identity: A cache object supplied through the client constructor is retained by identity and getCache() returns that same object as cache_identity.

This requirement covers only the cache object supplied through client construction and the `getCache()` result obtained from that same client. It does not address whether cache entries are hits, the source of the default cache, the OAuth endpoint, or the effects of auth client options on other authentication behavior.

The operation log should record the following in the order they occurred: whether the `Google_Client` constructor call was found; whether there was an actual cache argument; whether the left-hand side was the object actually passed into construction; whether the raw `getCache()` return value was obtained from the same client; and what was observed after comparing both sides. For the authentication portion, add only the options creation site, the order of entry into the call, and whether a comparison call exists. This lets the next review return to the specific objects rather than guessing again from names or cache misses.

## Issues not yet disentangled

The actual scope of auth client options has not been fully documented here. If the investigation continues, retain the location where the options are prepared, the order in which they enter `Google_Client`, and whether there is a comparison call without those options. Without this information, the authentication track cannot provide a causal explanation for the cache track.

The wrapper layer is also an adjacent boundary that has not yet been disentangled. The caller Fang Ke may save only the outer object before it is passed in, or may save only the outer object after `getCache()`. The former lacks the constructor argument, and the latter lacks the raw return value; identical class names, identical keys, or identical entry contents cannot fill either of these gaps.

## Appendix: How the old report was translated

"Cache miss" should be translated as an entry-level observation or an observation at the point of use, unless both ends of the object have already been compared. It can point to read/write order and entry state, but must not automatically lead to the identity-change branch.

"The return value is also a cache class" is merely a type record. Without constructor arguments and the original `getCache()` return value, it cannot serve as a conclusion about object relationships.

"A default cache exists" should be kept separate from "whether the call injects an object." The default pool can be used to continue checking calls with no visible arguments; when constructor input already exists, do not use the default path to invalidate that input.

"An authentication option is used" requires seeing at least where it is created or passed. When you see only `OAUTH2_AUTH_URL`, `OAUTH2_TOKEN_URI` or `OAUTH2_REVOKE_URI`, the record can say no more than that the client file provides a OAuth entry point.

## This Time's Goal and Historical Notes

This effort is to implement the remaining compatibility requirements for Compat Relay 2.19 on the frozen baseline `9016626`. The agreement on the current goal provided by the owner is the requirements source; missing implementation in the baseline, or old notes pointing to old classes or old versions, does not mean the goal is inapplicable. To verify a goal, ask the owner of the corresponding card to confirm that card's public calls and boundaries. Missing historical replay materials do not prevent the owner from providing the known contract. Some topics require designated related follow-up; chat will state the next step, while polling or unrelated messages do not advance these topics. Late reminders only point to existing contracts and do not promise additional historical artifacts.

# Response Header and Model Mapping Migration Procedure

This record began with a compatibility check for Compat Relay 2.19. Initially, two things needed to be checked together: repeated headers in responses and the model mapping callers relied on. They were grouped together because both can easily be treated as ordinary fields during migration; there is no evidence at this point that they should follow the same fix path.

## Early Migration Approach

The original investigation started at `src/Google/Service/Resource.php`. That location contains `Google_Service_Resource`, and the file imports `GuzzleHttp\Psr7\Request` at the top. Keep this as a reference point: first confirm which resource objects the request and response pass through, then check whether callers treat same-name headers as a single value. Do not replace the entire call chain after seeing only a class name.

The earliest working approach was to normalize the names, then take one usable value; if duplicate values appeared in practice, retain the raw response and let the caller decide. This was intended to avoid an immediate change to existing read logic, not to establish a confirmed long-term format. The same conservative approach was used for model mapping: retain the old mapping first, then pick a caller still in use and verify its version and entry point.

The sequence listed at the time was:

1. Pin down an existing test or example that produces repeated headers;
2. Use the resource object to confirm the location adjacent to the request;
3. Record whether the caller reads a single value or the raw response;
4. Check the actual model mapping version independently;
5. If the old caller's behavior cannot be explained, first revert to the pre-migration read behavior.

Here, "revert" only means that the caller continues reading with the old interpretation. It does not mean making a global rewrite within `Resource.php`.

## Notes Left During Review

A later review found that the initial use of "one usable value" as a compatibility result had conflated two things: whether reading one particular value was convenient, and whether the order of repeated values in the raw response was still intact. The former lets old callers keep running; it does not mean the latter has been preserved.

The resource class and the `Request` import only help locate the relevant code. They do not prove where headers are normalized, nor do they prove that model mapping differences come from the resource class. A short note remains in the review section: treat the path as navigation first, not as an attribution of cause. This reminder was kept because the early investigation did go off track for that reason.

One attempt collapsed same-name headers into a single value, then had callers retrieve the remaining values from the raw response. This did not become a migration plan. It required callers to understand two representations at once: ordinary reads used the collapsed value, while special reads went back to the raw response. This neither made the order of repeated values explicit nor avoided making callers guess whether they needed to retrieve additional values.

The old "take one usable value first" approach is therefore retained as a historical position, but should no longer be understood as a conclusion about repeated values.

## Model Mapping Branch

The model mapping check was not completed alongside the header review. The description of the difference has remained broad: a caller still in use gets different results in the current version. The known checks are the caller's actual version, entry point, and current result; the difference has not been attributed to the metadata itself or to request construction.

Do not add a nonexistent array rule to model mapping during migration just to make the two checks look symmetrical. It should retain its own samples: where the old mapping is still read, whether a change in the location of nullable affects the caller's decisions, and which results are merely surface effects of version differences. This branch remains unresolved on this page.

## Retained Recovery Options

If a caller being migrated only accepts single-value reads, it can continue using the pre-migration read interpretation initially, with that marked as the old path. Do not describe this temporary compatibility measure as a definition of the raw response.

If a caller relies on the existing shape of a mapping object, first restore the mapping entry point that caller originally used, then confirm again whether it depends on field presence, null handling, or version selection. Without this step, the supposed rollback will only tie two different problems together again.

What the next round needs is not more generic checks, but a concrete sample that distinguishes "only one value was retrieved" from "all values are still retained," plus a caller entry point that reproduces the model mapping difference.

# Response Header and Model Mapping Migration Process

This page started out as informal migration notes and was later used to trace compatibility changes in Compat Relay 2.19. It preserves several descriptions from different periods: some were merely ways to keep callers working at the time, while others were overturned by later reviews. Do not treat the old practices in the first half of the page directly as the current format definition.

## The Starting Point Left by 2023

The original scope was narrow: the response had repeated response headers, and there were also differences in model mapping compatibility. The two issues were recorded together not because they shared an implementation, but because they were encountered during the same migration effort. The early record had only one local entry point: `src/Google/Service/Resource.php`.

In the code frozen at the time, the object that could be located directly was `Google_Service_Resource`. The file header had `use GuzzleHttp\Psr7\Request;`. These two points allowed investigators to return to the area around the resource object and inspect where requests and responses were handed off. They did not specify the final shape in which a particular header was passed to callers, nor where the version difference in model mapping occurred.

The earliest working rule was written as "after normalizing the name, first take one available value." If the same-named header appeared multiple times, the raw response was left to special callers. The goal of this rule was practical: avoid rewriting all code that only read one value on the day of migration. It did not answer whether repeated values should be preserved, how they should be ordered, or who was responsible for interpreting them.

The original migration steps were also brief:

```text
Existing test or example
        |
        v
Request/response inspection near Google_Service_Resource
        |
        +-- Caller reads only one value: retain the old reading interpretation
        |
        +-- Caller needs repeated values: inspect the raw response
```

This diagram shows the old workflow, not the current behavior. It only expresses the manual investigation path used at the time, and in particular should not be used to prove that "inspect the raw response" is a stable interface.

The early notes also placed model mapping on the same checklist: find a caller still using the old mapping, and verify its actual version, entry point, and current result. At the time, no sample showed which field caused the difference; "the mapping changed" was merely an on-site description. To avoid turning speculation into a migration rule, the original record did not add an imagined set of conversion steps.

## A Reminder Written Beside the On-Call Notes

During the first review, the investigator left a simple note beside the resource class: the class name and import are only for locating it. This note remained useful because it blocked a very common leap—from the existence of `Google_Service_Resource` directly to the conclusion that all response handling was completed there.

The complete call chain was not traced at the time. This was not because its absence had been confirmed, but because these notes served only compatibility verification. The resource class was a point that could be revisited; the actual header-reading callers, wrapper layers, and test samples each required separate confirmation. The early documentation did not make this clear, which later led some people to treat the path itself as the conclusion.

Another marginal note concerned recovery: if a caller can handle only a single value, do not modify the resource object first and then wait for it to adapt; first let that caller retain its pre-migration reading interpretation. "Retain" was written too vaguely here, and later proved easy to misread as "discard the other values." The old wording is preserved because it explains why the original approach did not immediately push for a full replacement.

## The Compromise That Did Not Pass

The second review tried a compromise: same-named headers would still first be compressed into one value, and only callers identified as special would retrieve the remaining values from the raw response. It appeared to let old reads continue while leaving an escape hatch for cases that needed repeated values.

The actual problem was not whether the remaining values could be retrieved, but that the representation had been split. Ordinary callers received a compressed result, while special callers received a result from another source; there was no clear ordering relationship between the two, and it was not clear where name normalization occurred. If a caller later switched from ordinary reading to special reading, it did not receive a different view of the same data, but potentially two different interpretation paths.

This attempt did not become the migration plan. It was not removed from the history because it still illustrates the pressure at the time: old callers genuinely treated a single value as the norm, while repeated values could no longer be maintained by "manually returning to the raw response when necessary."

The same review also exposed a misjudgment. Someone had discussed the current-result difference in model mapping together with the header compromise, as if unifying the response representation on one side would cause the other side to recover automatically. There was no evidence supporting this connection. The mapping branch only established that the caller's version, entry point, and current result needed to be examined; it provided no evidence that could attribute the difference to the resource class, request object, or header normalization.

## Review Record from the Year of 2024

After the review, the old "first take one available value" rule received a limited correction. It could serve as a temporary reading method for old callers, but could no longer be called the compatibility definition for repeated headers. This change in wording was not because single-value reading had suddenly become invalid, but because it could not express the complete relationship among same-named values in the raw response.

An unfinished verification table was also retained at the time, with more detail than the original checklist:

| Object to inspect | Question that needed to be answered at the time | Conclusion that was not reached at the time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Repeated-header sample | Whether all same-named values were still visible before and after reading | What the unified representation was |
| Normalized name | Whether multiple occurrences mapped to the same name | Whether the name change affected ordering |
| Single-value caller | Whether it depended on the first value, any value, or the old interface shape | Whether it could move to the new representation without modification |
| Model mapping caller | Actual version, entry point, and current result | Which object caused the difference |

The last column was not filled in with definitive answers by later text. It reflects the gaps present during the review, not a completed acceptance checklist.

The migration order also changed during the review. Originally, the old callers were kept working first, followed by handling of special cases; later, the order was changed to fix the samples first and then determine whether callers could accept the representation change. The purpose was not to require all callers to migrate at once, but to first prevent "compatibility" from being reduced to a single conveniently readable value.

That review left no complete meeting minutes; the page retains only two conclusions. First, the resource-class path remains an entry point for tracing back, but is no longer responsible for attributing the implementation. Second, header and model mapping must be verified separately; appearing together in one migration does not make them a shared repair target.

## Deprecated Reading Method

The following is old content, preserved in its original sense, and is no longer applicable:

> If a same-named header appears multiple times, selecting one available value is sufficient; the remaining content is still in the raw response and can be retrieved by the caller when needed.

This reading method has two problems. It presents "select one" as an unconditional action without specifying the selection criteria; it also treats the raw response as a stable compensation channel exposed externally. For old code that handled only a single value, this text was once a temporary buffer statement; for the compatibility format after migration, it is insufficient to describe what must be preserved.

The old reading method was not removed entirely because some callers still operate under a single-value assumption. During migration, identify this assumption first rather than mistaking it for confirmed library behavior. If the old path needs to be restored temporarily, restore that caller's original interpretation and entry point; do not recompress the new representation into one value and call that a success.

## Model Mapping Was Not Merged Along with It

The model mapping record remains relatively thin. use Firebase\JWT\SignatureInvalidException;
use GuzzleHttp\Client;
use GuzzleHttp\ClientInterface;
