This page did not originally start from a complete client specification. It started with two issue terms that were easy to write on the same line: credential attachment / logger identity. The initial judgment on the ground was straightforward: Compat Relay 2.19 needed to be closed out, so first open `src/Google/Client.php`, check whether `Google_Client` was still there, and then inspect the authentication, cache, and HTTP-handling dependencies in the file header. Both issues could be entered from here, so the first version put them in the same round of checks.

That entry-point assessment has not become completely obsolete. `src/Google/Client.php:39` is `class Google_Client`, and nearby we can also see `LIBVER`, `USER_AGENT_SUFFIX`, `OAUTH2_REVOKE_URI`, `OAUTH2_TOKEN_URI`, `OAUTH2_AUTH_URL`, and `API_BASE_PATH`. The `ApplicationDefaultCredentials`, `MemoryCacheItemPool`, `CredentialsLoader`, and `HttpHandlerFactory` listed in the file header do indeed place credentials, caching, and request handling within the reading scope of the same file. It was reasonable for the old investigation to start here; the problem was that the next step was written too quickly.

The original decision was to use one "client upgrade check" to cover both issues. As long as `Google_Client` could be constructed and the authentication-related dependencies could still be found, credential attachment and logger identity were initially treated as pass items in the same round. The practical benefit of writing it this way was brevity: the first round did not need to distinguish caller results, diagnostic content, and repeated processing. It also left an obvious gap: successful construction only showed that the entry point was available. It did not show what credential attachment ultimately left for the caller, nor whether logger identity remained unchanged during the second processing.

The exact sentence in the early notes was: "logger identity can be confirmed together with credential attachment." That sentence was not deleted. It represents the working assumption at the time of the first version, not the checking standard adopted later. Keeping it also has a practical purpose: people following an old link can see why that round checked the client entry point only once but marked both issues as confirmed. If this history were simply polished into the current guidance, it would instead conceal the most important misreading in this requirements evolution.

## What the File Entry Point Can Tell Us

Reading downward from `Google_Client`, we can first confirm several adjacent objects. `CredentialsLoader` and `ApplicationDefaultCredentials` are credential-related names, `MemoryCacheItemPool` is a cache-related name, and `HttpHandlerFactory` is a name related to HTTP processing. They are useful for narrowing the reading scope. They cannot, based solely on their position in the file header, prove which object produced the specific credential attachment result, nor can they prove that the change in logger identity occurred at any particular layer of credential loading, caching, or the HTTP handler.

Likewise, public constants were not treated as a unified form of identity proof. `LIBVER` and `USER_AGENT_SUFFIX` describe content near the client's public identifiers; several OAuth addresses and `API_BASE_PATH` are endpoint or path constants. Earlier records grouped these names under "client identity." That was useful for searching filenames, but too broad for determining logger identity. During the later follow-up, these object names were retained but downgraded to entry-point clues rather than result criteria.

This is also why this page does not infer implementation ownership directly from any dependency name. What can currently be confirmed is the declarations in the file, the direct dependencies in the file header, and the follow-up entry point starting from that file. As for the specific location in the call chain where credential attachment is completed, or why logger identity differs during repeated processing, the available material does not provide enough implementation relationships. Adjacent relationships are not written here as causal relationships.

## Two Options Became Two Observation Surfaces

When the material was reorganized later, the comparison was not a completely new grand design, but three existing approaches:

| Approach | What it leaves behind | Gap it exposes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Only confirm that `Google_Client` can be constructed | The client entry point is still usable | No caller result for credential attachment, and no repeated processing |
| Use the internal authentication name as the regression | Easy to investigate starting from the file header | Tied to names such as `CredentialsLoader`, which cannot replace the external result |
| Record the two items separately | A separate place for the result and repeated processing | Requires recording the processing once more |

The first approach was not completely rejected. It can still serve as the starting point for manual reading: open `src/Google/Client.php`, and confirm whether `Google_Client`, the public constants, and the file-header dependencies still lead to the same entry point. It simply cannot, by itself, close out both issues. The second approach also retains value for locating things, but the existence of a name cannot be written as a passing regression. The decision was to adopt the third approach and separate "where to start looking" from "what result counts as recorded."

After GAPI-211 appeared, the observation target for credential attachment became clear. It required adding a repository regression for the upgraded result and asserting the user-visible result rather than an internal helper-function name. This change did not specify a particular function in `Client.php`, nor did it make `CredentialsLoader` a required fixed implementation name. It only moved the regression record from "whether a particular internal name is still there" to "whether the result obtained by the caller still holds."

GAPI-228 address the other side. Logger identity must be processed once and then again separately, with a record of whether the content or diagnostics remain stable. The absence of an exception during one processing cannot automatically establish that the second processing is also stable; likewise, observing the expected result for credential attachment cannot replace the repeated-processing record for logger identity. The two items share the client entry point and the compatibility closeout context, but the evidence they leave behind is not the same type.

Therefore, the scope of the Compat Relay 2.19 decision was narrowed to two points: the credential attachment regression uses the callerFang Kevisible result as its subject; the logger identity follow-up must retain a comparison between the first and second processing. This decision did not reassign a module owner for `src/Google/Client.php`, nor did it derive a complete call graph from the file-header dependencies.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ClientFile
    ClientFile --> SplitObservation
    SplitObservation --> CredentialResult
    SplitObservation --> LoggerRepeat
```

In the diagram, `ClientFile` only indicates that, starting from `src/Google/Client.php`, `SplitObservation` means splitting the two observations. `CredentialResult` corresponds to the callerFang Kevisible result, and `LoggerRepeat` corresponds to the comparison between the first and second processing. It does not indicate that a particular dependency owns the implementation, nor does it combine the two observations into one pass condition.

## The Cache Aside Was Not Closed Out

`MemoryCacheItemPool` was listed in one review as an object that might need further investigation. This aside was not ultimately expanded into a causal judgment, because the current material only confirms that it appears among the direct dependencies in the file header. It cannot be used to write that "the credential attachment result comes from the cache," nor can it explain whether logger identity is stable.

Earlier wording also showed a tendency to say that "clearing the cache first is enough to determine attachment." That merely mistook a visible dependency for processing causality and cannot be treated as an operational decision made on this page. The discussion related to `scoped cache keys` remains in DOC-21; DOC-20 do not carry over that set of candidate rules. The boundary to retain here is simply this: cache names can guide reading, but cannot replace the caller result or the repeated-processing observation.

`HttpHandlerFactory` follows the same boundary. It is an object encountered when reading from the file header, but that does not mean every logger identity phenomenon occurs inside the HTTP handler. The presence of `ApplicationDefaultCredentials` alone also cannot prove that it completed a particular credential attachment. The old draft strung several adjacent names into an implicit call chain. That construction was later withdrawn, but the related names remain in the history to explain where the old judgment came from.

## The Entry Point Left by Each of the Two Cards

The local description of GAPI-211 is "add a repository regression for credential attachment that asserts the user-visible result rather than an internal helper-function name." Therefore, its role on this page is to provide the entry point for stating the result: when this card is encountered, return to the caller result instead of continuing to pile up assertions around internal names.

The local description of GAPI-228 requires separately performing the first and second processing for logger identity and recording whether the content or diagnostics remain stable. Its role is to provide the entry point for repeated processing: when this card is encountered, first confirm that there really were two observations; do not cite only one successful result. Both cards relate to the old entry point of `src/Google/Client.php`, but the cards themselves do not provide material for attributing the phenomenon to a particular dependency, and this page does not add that attribution.

DOC-21 records token expiry fallback / scoped cache keys, which share adjacent client context with this page's credential attachment / logger identity. The two pages can link to each other, but they do not share one set of conclusions. In particular, the fact that `MemoryCacheItemPool` also appears in the file header does not allow the candidate rules for token cache to be written as this page's decision.

## Outdated Sections

> Old wording: Because the authentication-related dependencies were still present, logger identity could be treated as an incidental confirmation of credential attachment.
>
> Later addendum: No longer applicable. The dependencies remaining only shows that the names near the entry point have not disappeared; whether the first and second processing are stable must be recorded separately.

> Old wording: `LIBVER` and `USER_AGENT_SUFFIX` were sufficient to represent client identity and could therefore be used to determine all identity-related phenomena.
>
> Later addendum: The scope was too broad. They are constants near the client's public identifiers and cannot replace observation of the diagnostic object's identity.

> Old wording: Once `MemoryCacheItemPool` was seen, the change in attachment could first be handled as being caused by the cache.
>
> Later addendum: This was not confirmed. Adjacency in the file header is insufficient to support that causal judgment, so the old wording is not currently used as a basis for action.

These sections were not cleaned up into a new authoritative guide. They preserve three reading biases: treating a shared entry point as a shared failure, treating a public identifier as diagnostic identity, and treating a dependency name as cache causality. The later decision changed only the observation method; it did not erase the time trail of these old standards.

## Decision Retained

The final wording adopted on this page is: the credential attachment regression asserts the user-visible result and is not tied to an internal helper-function name; logger identity requires separate records of the content or diagnostic comparison for the first and second processing. `src/Google/Client.php` and `Google_Client` remain verification entry points, while file-header dependencies and public constants serve only as adjacent clues. GAPI-211 and GAPI-228 navigate to the two observation surfaces respectively and do not replace each other.

This is the part of the current history that can be reused directly. The parts that remain unresolved are also left unchanged: there is no material showing that the credential attachment result must be attributed to a particular file-header dependency, and no material showing which internal layer causes the logger identity difference. If a specific implementation relationship is added later, it should be recorded separately; this page continues to serve as the history of the options, the old judgment, the correction path, and how the two observations were separated.

# Token Fallback and Cache Key Adjustment Proposal

Consider token expiry fallback and scoped cache keys separately first. Both are close to credential handling, but the former concerns whether expired content can still be used, while the latter concerns the scope of cache identity. If both are changed at once, it will be hard to tell which change caused any differences in repeated processing.

The current entry point for investigation is `src/Google/Client.php`. The file contains `Google_Client`, `LIBVER`, `USER_AGENT_SUFFIX`, and the OAuth address constant. It also imports the `CredentialsLoader`, `MemoryCacheItemPool`, and HTTP handlers at the top. This is a useful place to continue tracing, but the entry point alone does not establish where the expiry check or cache key actually belongs.

The initial recommendation is to keep the existing cache identity and observe only the first and repeat processing of the same input. Record the content or diagnostics from both runs, then decide whether to try scoped cache keys on their own.

To confirm: which layer the expiry state is read from; whether fallback writes back to the original cache object; whether the caller supplies the cache identity.

# Token Fallback and Cache Key Adjustment Proposal

After review, do not combine token expiry fallback and scoped cache keys into a single "cache fix." The two efforts are related, but they answer different questions: fallback determines when the contents of stored credentials can no longer be used, while scoped cache keys determine whether different contexts receive the same cache identity. If both areas change in the first pass, differences in repeated processing will have no comparable baseline.

`src/Google/Client.php` remains the entry point for follow-up. It declares `Google_Client` and lists `LIBVER`, `USER_AGENT_SUFFIX`, `OAUTH2_REVOKE_URI`, `OAUTH2_TOKEN_URI`, `OAUTH2_AUTH_URL`, and `API_BASE_PATH`. The file header shows the introduction of `ApplicationDefaultCredentials`, `MemoryCacheItemPool`, `CredentialsLoader`, and `HttpHandlerFactory`. It identifies adjacent locations related to credentials, caching, and requests, but these declarations alone cannot determine where expiry is checked or which fields make up the scoped key.

## Try the two candidates in sequence

**Candidate A: Organize only the fallback observation surface.**

Keep the existing cache identity unchanged, and run the same input through first and repeated processing. Record each result as content, a diagnostic, or indeterminate, and mark whether the second result changed. Record the credential-content fields `created`, `expires_in`, `value`, and `expired` used for the determination alongside the result, so that seeing only "the second result differed" does not lead to attributing the cause to the cache key.

The advantage of this candidate is its small change surface and its ability to establish a comparison for repeated processing first. Its limitation is also clear: even if both results are stable, that only shows that this input set did not expose a scope difference; it does not establish that scoped cache keys are problem-free.

**Candidate B: Try only scoped cache keys.**

Treat the cache identity scope as an independent variable and do not use it to address token expiry yet. Change only identity inputs that already exist on each run, while keeping the same processing-result records as in Candidate A. The available material does not specify the key's field combination, so do not assume account, request, or other dimensions, and do not present temporarily assembled fields as public interface requirements.

Candidate B may expose insufficient scope, but it may also only bypass expired content. If the token has expired, changing only the key cannot prove that fallback is handled correctly, so it cannot replace Candidate A.

**Candidate C: Try both at the same time.**

Do not adopt this yet. It may shorten a single trial, but a successful result would not show whether the expiry check changed the outcome or the cached object selected by the key changed it; a failure would likewise not preserve a reusable counterexample. Unless A and B each have a stable comparison, do not make C the merge direction.

## Recording format and interface cost

The observation method for token expiry fallback in GAPI-212 is first and repeated processing of the same object, with a record of whether the content or diagnostic is stable. The actual record does not need to expand into a full cache test suite. Next to the two processing runs, state clearly: whether the input is the same, whether the same cache identity was used, whether the return value is content or a diagnostic, and how the second run differs from the first.

If the two runs are the same, retain that result first; do not interpret it as proof that the cache scope is already correct. If they differ, trace the credential content and expiry check first, then decide whether to proceed to Candidate B. Record cache scope as a separate item, stating whether this round kept the same cache identity; if the scope changed because of an existing input, also record the point of change. This keeps the fallback sample from being obscured by the key discussion.

This trial does not add a public configuration option. If the caller has already supplied a cache object or identity, fallback must not silently replace it with another unidentifiable scope; otherwise, even a stable result will leave the caller unable to explain the cache's origin. If the existing identity is in fact insufficient to isolate contexts that need to be distinguished, the change should explicitly address cache identity semantics rather than using an expired token as a blanket justification.

## Stop conditions

If any of the following occurs, stop treating scoped cache keys as a fallback patch and return to observing one item at a time:

- The caller's existing cache identity must be changed to obtain a stable result;
- The difference between two runs of the same input still cannot be explained by the credential content and expiry state;
- A change in key scope obscures the diagnostic instead of making the two runs easier to compare;
- A new public parameter is required, but it is unclear whether it addresses expiry or isolation.

What remains undecided is the exact read point for the expiry check, whether fallback touches an existing cached object, and the minimum identity boundary for scoped cache keys. Do not commit to Candidate B's interface shape until Candidate A's comparison is established.

## Three Directions on the Old Note

The first direction was to handle it based on the filename. Because `MediaFileUpload` matched both resumable and response, it was casually treated as the sole source of the return format. This direction seemed fastest, but it directly replaced the "investigation entry point" with "implementation ownership." A file location can help someone find the code, but it cannot prove that the result will not be received, replaced, or rethrown by an outer layer.

The second direction was to add a unified conversion layer in advance inside the upload class. The reason in favor was that the caller Fang Ke would have one fewer difference to handle; the reason against it was also specific: at the time, it was unknown whether the thing to convert was the return object, the response body, or an exception. If it were wrapped first, content that the caller could originally see might be hidden; if one object type were selected first, behavior that had not yet been observed would be written as a compatibility promise.

The third direction was to walk through the call adjacency once and retain only the two types of content that actually occurred. For normal completion, look at what the caller received; for failure or interruption, look at what the caller actually saw. This direction was adopted. It made no promise to "preserve the original" and no promise that "the upload layer would not change"; it only fixed the order of decisions: see the content first, then discuss whether conversion is needed.

The subsequent review still began from `Google_Http_MediaFileUpload`, but the role of the entry point was described more narrowly. The file header shows:

```php
use GuzzleHttp\\Psr7;
use GuzzleHttp\\Psr7\\Request;
use GuzzleHttp\\Psr7\\Uri;

```

# Caller Integration Entry Point Migration Index

This index is organized by consumer first, not by directory name. Call samples from clients and examples go on the same row, alongside the replacement location, callers still using the entry point, and the original inputs or failure symptoms that show what happened at the time. Google · Client Integration has its own schedule and handover arrangements, so similarly named entry points from the main project must not be folded in.

The old draft treated `OAuth callback` and splitting out `service package` as two candidate paths. That assessment has not been removed: it explains why the old entry point was not declared retired outright at the time. Records added later did not automatically make the two paths the same thing either; this page records only callers that were actually migrated and the replacement locations they moved to.

## How to Write Index Rows

Each row must retain at least the following fields. A blank does not mean "no issues"; it only means the information has not yet been checked with the caller.

| Field | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| Old entry point | Where the caller originally entered; give similarly named side paths their own rows. |
| Replacement location | An entry point that has been tried, or an object that has been split out; do not substitute a newly created name in the directory. |
| Caller | Clients or examples confirmed to still be using it; do not add unconfirmed names. |
| Batch | The consumers being migrated in this batch, and the inputs and first observed behavior recorded before migration. |
| Rollback trace | Why the old entry point was restored, and the results of rechecking after restoration; if there was no rollback, do not invent a success note. |

"Current" in the index means the entry point a caller is actually using at that moment, not the four Chinese characters for "current entry point" in the title. Append any late-added current entry point in its original chronological order, and note that it did not change the existing situation; this is also required by GAPIA-013. Do not move it back into an old batch just to make the table look tidy.

```text
Before migration
Caller ──> Old entry point
             │ Keep the original input and first observed behavior

After trial
Same caller ──> Replacement location
             │ Restore the old entry point on a mismatch

After confirmation
Caller ──> Replacement location
Keep the old entry point only for callers not yet migrated or for rollback
```

## Change Only One Caller per Migration

First, find a caller in the index that you can still confirm, and copy down its original entry point, input, and first observed failure. Then change only that caller's entry point. Do not also change the input, caller population, or other surrounding conditions. Only then is the state on the second call comparable.

Keep the old entry point available during the trial. A replacement location appearing in the directory, or an example that can already be opened, is not enough to show that the old entry point can be shut down. Migration is complete only when all three conditions can be verified locally: the caller has actually used the replacement location; the caller confirms it no longer depends on the old entry point; and a history query can still find the entry point record saved before this migration. If any one is missing, keep the caller listed under the old entry point.

Earlier, green screenshots were also included in the trial notes; that practice was later dropped. The cleaned-up screenshots do not show the original inputs or failure exit points and cannot be used to assess a migration. The index treats local fix output only as a diagnostic attachment; the public entry point rechecks in GAPIA-015 followed the same rule.

If a caller wants to move from `OAuth callback` to somewhere else, first enter the actual replacement location in that row. `service package` may appear only when it really is the destination for this call; do not fill it in across the board just because the old draft listed it as a candidate. The callers still using `deferred request` have not yet been fully verified, so they are not being included in migration batches yet.

## Rechecks, Anomalies, and Restoration

Start rechecks at the public entry point. First check whether collection and execution are both enabled. In GAPIA-017, the collection status of google-client-int differed from that of the current entry point; without evidence, do not fill in zeros or write "disabled" for "not collected." Once the status is confirmed, check the same caller's first and second results at the replacement location.

When the second result changes, stop at that row rather than expanding to other callers. Existing records show that the second result has changed before without the original expiry action changing along with it; that change needs to stay in the index's rollback trace and should not be overwritten by a new recheck. If `token cache` shows an inconsistency, restore the old entry point, reuse the original input for another check, and keep the differences observed before and after restoration in that caller's row.

Restoring the old entry point does not mean never trying again after a failed migration. It just puts the caller back on a known path until the replacement location and the state of the second call can be checked again. Do not delete the trial records while restoring it; whoever takes over later needs to know what was changed and at which step it was rolled back.

## Old Paths Still in Use

Rows for old entry points do not close automatically as time passes. Move them from "still in use" to "migrated out" only when the replacement location, caller confirmation, and history query can all be verified. Keep any notes that cannot be verified marked as outdated, and note alongside them whether the missing piece is the caller, replacement location, or original observed behavior. Do not guess to fill in the gaps.

The handover records in GAPIA-019 require following the actual action routing to find the person taking over. Remove retired groups from the new entry point; do not keep treating them as post-migration contacts. DOC-28 records a case where the same object appeared in two states; when this happens, first keep the state records and entry point records separate. Do not infer from just one state that the other entry point has completed migration.

Related cards: GAPIA-013, GAPIA-015, GAPIA-017, GAPIA-019.

# Quality Signal Console: Temporary Coverage Boundaries

Temporary coverage is short-lived: someone needs to complete an exit action, but domain-specific judgment about the object in question remains with the original maintenance chain. The table below does not combine those two responsibilities under one person or fill a vacant long-term role with the temporary on-call person.

`docs/adj-license/ownership/adj-license-temporary-takeover-boundaries.md` is this page's project entry point. It records the scope of coverage; the body and attachments are still maintained by LICENSE · Quality Signal Board.

## Objects and Routing

| Incoming item | First contact | What they can handle | Where to stop |
|---|---|---|---|
| An exit action is due | Temporary maintainer | Verify and complete this one due action | Do not explain why the action arose |
| Explanation of license-quality-signal behavior | Original owner | The original owner determines the signal's meaning and attribution | The temporary maintainer only passes along the observed details |
| Failure samples produced by test | Original owner | Determine which regression layer or instability signal the sample belongs to | Leave blank if there is no long-term maintainer |
| Changes in regression-layer ownership | Relevant maintainer | Append a new ownership assessment | Do not overwrite the old assessment |
| Incoming items that cannot be matched to a known object | Project entry point | Record the incoming item and its due time | Do not answer on behalf of the domain owner |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Exit action received] --> B{Only handling the due action?}
    B -- Yes --> C[Temporary maintainer handles it]
    B -- No --> D[Original owner]
    D --> E{Long-term role known?}
```

# On-call procedure for a failed docs site run

This page still retains the old response sequence from one failed docs site run. It is useful for capturing the state first when you receive a message such as "the entry point looks wrong"; it is not a basis for attributing all release note issues to the same cause. This run covers the user-facing entry point for model-documentation-portal, along with the release notes and outdated content visible beside it.

When you begin, preserve the original page first. Keep the entry URL, the result currently displayed on the page, and the sequence in which you first observed the anomalies. Do not refresh immediately, do not clear the shared cache, and do not paste notes from another export run back onto the page. If the page later recovers or links are later added, record those separately as subsequent states.

## Old first-pass procedure

1. Open the entry point on the docs site from `docs/adj-model/runbooks/Model-metadata-and-mapping-user-resource-hub-failed-run-on-call-page.md`.
2. Confirm that the page is the docs site's user-facing entry point, then follow the links on the page.
3. Stop at the first broken link, outdated content, or current result you cannot explain.
4. Record where you stopped, what the entry point displays, and which actions have not yet been performed in this run.

This sequence came from an early run, when the only requirement was to find the first point where you could not continue. It did not require the person on call to prove why the page was wrong or to remove all outdated content in the same run. The old record treated "the entry point still has the old value" primarily as residual cached data; that judgment later turned out not to be reliable enough. It is retained here to explain why no further rerun was made at the time.

## First distinguish the three page results

Just because the entry page opens does not mean the release notes it references are from this export run. Correct-looking release notes also do not mean all outdated content has been dealt with. Conversely, a broken link only shows that the current path is broken at that point; it cannot by itself establish that all content on the docs site is unavailable.

It's best to write the on-call log in the following order:

| Object observed | What to record | Immediate action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| User-facing entry point | Original URL and initial result | Preserve the page; do not replace the link |
| Release notes | Whether the content is still as expected | Compare only one object with the most recent known-good sample |
| Outdated content | Where it first appeared | Do not clean it up as a side task in this run |
| Exit action | Differences between the original and second environments | Leave for cross-environment verification |

If there is no recent known-good sample, stop at "unable to compare"; do not use a page from another environment as the normal baseline. If no page object is available, do not just write "docs site issue" either; at minimum, record whether the entry point, release notes, or outdated content was the first to differ.

## Stop points for this run

In the reproduction record for GAPIC-008, the path stopped at the first broken link, and the current result was not explained further. Use the same stopping point: anyone other than the original author should follow the existing entry point and stop if any item is missing or at the first difference. Change only one condition per comparison; for example, change only the viewing environment or only the known-good sample, not both at once.

GAPIC-007 previously recorded that the current entry point still had the old value after the window ended. The old page attributed this directly to stale cache data; do not act on that conclusion now. First record that the window had ended, then check whether the content displayed at the current entry point comes from an old task or stale cache data; record these two cases separately in the incident notes. If no page result can distinguish the two, leave it unconfirmed.

GAPIC-015 previously flagged differences after a cold start. If a rerun is needed, clear only your own cache, then check the current entry point again; do not touch the shared cache. Before rerunning, record the original entry point and result, and put the new result on a separate line after the rerun. Returning to normal after a cold start does not erase the original broken link.

## Cross-environment handling

GAPIC-011 is used to verify the exit action. Before entering the second environment, finish recording the first failure point in the original environment. The second environment only answers whether a new divergence appears between the exit action and the docs site page; it is not a substitute sample for the original environment.

The sample attached later showed that the execution record could be reconstructed, but the section on the current result came from an old image. If you encounter the same situation, keep it marked as an old image; do not treat the image contents as facts about the page in the original environment. If the original environment can no longer be viewed, the handoff log should explicitly state "the original result could not be viewed again"; do not fill in details based on the image.

## When to hand it off

On the docs site side, continue to preserve the user-facing entry point, release notes, outdated content, and the first failure the user saw. If the difference extends beyond these objects—for example, if you need to determine why the shared interface provided different content—hand off the entry point and observed behavior along with the original record; this page makes no further inferences about implementation causes.

The handoff should include: the original entry point, the first page object that differed, the single comparison performed, hypotheses that have been ruled out or have not yet been verified, and where the next shift can pick up. GAPIC-004 can be used to check whether a record was kept before switching environments; GAPIC-011 can be used to continue cross-environment verification of the exit action. Do not treat the card status as evidence that the page has recovered.

## Retained legacy rollback section

The early rollback instructions required restoring the state via the old entry point. That entry point is still useful for checks under different permissions, but is no longer guaranteed to represent a normal page. If a rollback is necessary now, restore only to the entry-point record preserved before this run began, and show the post-rollback page result alongside the original result. Continue to mark recovery actions that have not been validated in the shared environment as untried.

The last addendum to this page did not remove all the old judgments: the old entry point, the old image, and the claim that "old value means cache" can still help readers understand the earlier response, but cannot on their own serve as conclusions for a new run.

```text
Replacement location during migration
```

This sequence was once used as the completion criterion: once the replacement location could handle `.github/workflows` and had gone through one rollback window, maintenance of the old entry point could stop. At the time, the build queue continuing to run was treated as a sign that caller migration was complete. This criterion has not been deleted, because existing records were archived under it; it also did not list all compatible callers.

Rollback observations later added in the margin changed the operational priorities. When a rollback occurs, no longer treat it as an opportunity to expand the migration; restore the old entry point first. Here, "restore" only means returning the caller to its original entry point. It does not mean artifact versions automatically return to their previous state, nor that the build queue will cancel work already queued. The old version lumped these actions together as one "rollback," which made for easy reading but made it easy to miss the records left by release when carrying out the steps.

The index still uses the old names and sections. It has not designated the replacement location as the sole entry point, nor has it recorded the last confirmation from every consumer. Migration batches can only be tracked per caller: one caller moving to the replacement location does not establish the status of another caller; one artifact version going through a rollback window does not establish the status of later versions.

1. In the index, find where this caller originally pointed to `service-release-automation`.
2. Check whether it has been entered under the replacement location. If there is only a directory link and no caller record, continue to treat it as using the old entry point.

# Compatibility Freeze Decision Record

The conclusion left in the initial draft was brief: retain the existing compat entry point, and revisit the compatibility window later. That sentence was sufficient at the end of the meeting, but it compressed two distinct judgments into one. Whether the entry point should continue to exist was a decision that could be made in this round; whether the window should be adjusted depended on migration judgments that had not yet been separated out. In later reviews, the brief conclusion was often read as "there is no problem with the window; it just has not been scheduled yet," which was not what was actually approved at the time.

This addendum preserves the original decision as well as the issues that were unresolved at the time. It is not an overarching rule for subsequent compatibility work. If a different window strategy has since been established, it must not be retroactively described as an outcome that this freeze had already anticipated.

## The two paths presented at the meeting

The first path was to maintain the current compat entry point and limit the freeze to the requests and responses observable in the existing material. This did not promise that callers had already migrated, nor did it fix the meaning of the window in advance. The cost was equally clear: the entry point would remain, and discussion of the window would not automatically disappear once the freeze was complete.

The second path was to adjust the compatibility window first, then interpret existing calls using the new window. Supporters hoped to clear up ambiguities around the old entry point sooner, so that subsequent material would not continue to accumulate around a temporary boundary. The objection was not that the window could never change, but that the existing material did not map changes in calls to visible requests and responses one by one. If a window change were announced first, different results appearing later could be attributed either to changed compat behavior or to callers not having migrated yet; the two explanations would obscure each other.

The meeting adopted the first path. Here, "retain" is a freeze action, not a guarantee covering every consequence of the old entry point; "defer" is not an already approved migration plan either. The initial draft described the window as "posing no risk for now." That earlier judgment is retained as background, but no longer applies. At the time, we did not have enough records to assess the level of risk; we could only determine that it should not be folded into the freeze scope that was already supported.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Current compat entry point] --> B[Observable requests and responses]
    B --> C[compatibility facts]
    B --> D[migration assumptions]
    D --> E[Compatibility window adjustment]
```

The separation in the diagram is not an implementation sequence, nor does it require callers to immediately do two sets of work. It expresses the order of judgment during review: first acknowledge what is externally visible, then discuss which statements are merely inferences about migration. If the window interpretation and existing behavior were previously written together, overturning any one assumption would also leave the observed results without a clear place in the account.

## What green results could establish at the time

The meeting material retains this original statement:

> "A green job without its input and exit-code record is treated as incomplete evidence."

This statement did not change the job's status. A green result remained a work signal, indicating that the execution did not end in an obvious failure; what changed was how much explanatory weight a green result could carry in this decision. Without an input record, reviewers could not know which compat path the run covered or map it back to a particular request and response. Without a exit-code record, they could not confirm how the execution ended or whether the outer workflow had masked a state that otherwise needed explanation.

Therefore, the shorthand "green means we can proceed" in the initial draft should no longer be used literally. Green can remain in the material, but it is not, by itself, evidence for extending the scope. When using a run as a basis for the freeze, the input that triggered it and its exit status need to be visible; when those records are missing, the correct response is to reduce its explanatory weight, not to presume that unseen details were normal.

Nor does "input" here mean every environmental detail, and exit-code is certainly not being treated as a substitute indicator of migration success. Their purpose in this decision is narrow: to allow an execution to be traced back to the request, response, and ending state discussed at the time. Without these two reference points, a green result can still help identify work progress, but it cannot independently answer whether the compatibility boundary has been covered.

One proposal was to treat a green job directly as substitute evidence for adjusting the window. It was not adopted. The reason was not that the job was useless, but that the color did not come with enough context. Even if the records were completed later, the run result could only become one piece of reviewable material; it would not automatically elevate assumptions about migration into compatibility facts.

## Freeze visible behavior first

Another working sequence was repeatedly quoted in the meeting:

> "Freeze the observable request and response first, then separate compatibility facts from assumptions about the migration."

Here, observable refers only to the requests and responses that could already be seen through execution and review material at the time. It does not mean freezing the entire internal implementation, nor does it mean making a complete commitment for future migration. The purpose of retaining the existing compat entry point is to give this round an external boundary that can be checked, not to turn the entry point into an unchangeable permanent object.

Listing migration assumptions separately does not mean migration is unimportant. Quite the opposite: whether a window adjustment is justified still depends on these judgments; they simply did not have material of equal strength in this round. Once separated, subsequent discussion can clearly distinguish whether it is examining existing compatibility behavior or inferences about the migration path. The former can be retained and the latter revised, without requiring both to be declared correct or incorrect together.

The review did not add a conclusion that "migration is now feasible." What it restored was the boundary of the original decision: observed behavior and migration interpretations that still need validation should not be mixed together in the text. An additional review cannot justify rewriting a premise that originally lacked evidence as a fact already approved by the meeting.

## Why the review starting point was retained

Early discussion followed `src/Google/Client.php` and several call names. This location served a practical purpose at the time: it let participants return from a stable entry point to the call relationships around compat, rather than arguing only over the abstract word "window." It also helped confirm that retaining the entry point and adjusting the window were not the same change; the former could be treated as an existing object within this round's freeze, while the latter required a separate explanation.

The file location is not the permanent home of this decision. If a later review starts from another call site, "not starting from Client.php" must not be interpreted as a departure from the decision made at the time. The path is retained here only because the checks at the time did in fact start there. Responsibility for compatibility, visible behavior, and migration judgments were not all confined to this one source location.

The initial draft also said that "leaving the entry point unchanged is enough to avoid risk." This, too, was shorthand that helped bring the meeting to a close, and should not continue to be quoted later. Retaining the entry point can only avoid introducing both window changes and changes to the existing entry point in the same round; it cannot replace review of requests, responses, input records, and exit status. Retaining the entry point was the selected action, not a guarantee covering every impact.

## Approaches that were not adopted

Besides directly adjusting the window, a faster approach also came up during review: first write an interpretation based on the new window, then gradually fill in the subsequent material. This appeared to allow migration discussion to begin earlier, but it would place a provisional interpretation ahead of visible behavior. If a caller later obtained a different result, maintainers would not be able to determine from the final text alone whether it reflected the existing compat entry point's behavior, the effect of a window change, or an original migration assumption that did not hold.

This path was not included in the decision, not because it was impossible to implement, but because the material it required was not available at the time. The purpose of recording it is to explain why the window was not adjusted directly, not to predetermine the answer for the next discussion. If it is attempted again later, at a minimum, the two layers separated at the time will need to be mapped back to each other: one is the requests and responses already observed, and the other is the assumptions about migration and their validation.

Someone also suggested first treating the window change as a reclassification in the text, leaving the entry point unchanged, and then using a green job to prove that the new classification was usable. This proposal likewise fell outside the approved scope. Renaming does not eliminate unexplained differences between calls and external behavior; if the explanation still relies on a migration assumption, it cannot be written as a completed compatibility judgment.

## What this decision actually approved

This round approved retaining the current compat entry point and freezing the requests and responses covered by the existing material. For these items, reviewers should be able to trace back to execution records containing inputs and exit status. Green jobs without those records may still be mentioned, but only as an incomplete basis; they cannot independently expand the approved scope.

This round did not approve adjusting the compatibility window, nor did it approve using migration assumptions to fill in the meaning of the window. Discussion of migration may continue, but it should be recorded separately from observed compatibility facts. The purpose is not to reduce discussion, but to allow subsequent material to retract a specific assumption precisely, without also having to reject requests or responses that have already been seen.

The decision did not state that "all callers have completed migration," because there was no material supporting that statement at the time. Nor did it list every possible situation in a risk table; that would make this limited decision appear more complete than the information actually available. Only one unresolved point remains: whether the compatibility window can be adjusted without changing existing visible behavior. The initial draft raised this question, and the review still did not turn it into a conclusion.

## How to read the record after this addendum

This review mainly checked whether the initial draft mixed evidence with assumptions. The result is that "retain the entry point and revisit the window later" needs to be read as two separate statements: retaining the entry point is this round's decision; whether to adjust the window later is only a direction that remains to be validated. The former can be supported by this round's material; the latter cannot be treated as an approved follow-up action simply because it sounds reasonable.

The old page is still retained because it records why the window change was not included in the freeze, not because it can replace compatibility documentation developed later. For handoff background on the CI evidence window, see DOC-44; that page addresses the handoff itself and does not change the approved scope here.

One related question has not been separated out: if the input record is already sufficient to identify an execution, but the interpretation of the response still depends on a migration assumption, should that execution be included in the next round of window discussion? The current record has no answer. It can only establish that, within this round's freeze, such unseparated material cannot be used to replace retention of the existing compat entry point.

# Release Handoff Entry Point Code Walkthrough

During review, keep the public release entry point, one direct caller, and the rollback checklist on the same reading path. This avoids starting with a broad search across release-related directories: directories can contain same-named files, and similar names don't mean they participate in the release train handoff.

```text
public release entry point
        |
   direct caller identified by the entry point
        |
first consumer of the release train handoff
```

Start at the public entry point and record the direct caller it explicitly points to. For the next hop, check only who first receives the object this caller hands off; that object's first consumer is the stopping point for this trace. Here, "first" is determined by call edges, not by filenames, directory depth, or search result order.

The rollback checklist is only a navigation aid on this path. It can indicate which rollback actions near the handoff need attention, so it is useful for cross-checking the transition between the entry point and the caller. It cannot, on its own, prove that a same-named object is the consumer, and the checklist should not be expanded into a release review.

After review, these two locations were not documented as the handoff's permanent home: they only help recover the context of that investigation. title: Dependency Mirror Maintenance Deviation Postmortem

versions.body:
# Dependency Mirror Maintenance Discrepancy Review

This record covers a discrepancy during a dependency mirror maintenance window. The visible results did not match the original plan. The immediate priority was to determine whether maintenance could continue, then distinguish confirmed observations from causes that still lacked evidence. This page preserves the judgments made at the time rather than turning them into a reusable operating procedure after the fact.

## Timeline

- When the checks first showed an anomaly, the record was only sufficient to confirm that the observed result differed from what the original plan expected. This was not recorded as proof that the mirror contents were corrupted, nor was a single result used to assign responsibility.
- The investigation traced back through `src/Google/Client.php` and related call names. That location served as an entry point for the investigation at the time; it was not established as the permanent home of the discrepancy. Source locations and coordination arrangements for the maintenance window are separate matters on this page.
- A temporary recovery allowed the window to proceed. The recovery showed that the immediate blocker could be worked around, not that the root cause of the original discrepancy had been found. The recovery action cannot be treated as a long-term fix either.
- The PHP deprecation transcript was retained after recovery. It was one of the raw artifacts observed at the time; the record did not recast its messages as a stronger conclusion of failure.

## Impact on the Window

The first impact was on maintenance decisions: until the results could be reconciled with the plan, this part of the work could not be signed off on merely because it "looked normal." The temporary recovery reduced the immediate pause but did not resolve questions about the input, execution results, and exit status for the subsequent handoff. The recorded impact of this discrepancy is therefore limited to the maintenance results visible within the window; it does not extend to a claim that the entire client, service package, or callers were affected.

The control added at the time was that a green `A green job without its input and exit-code record is treated as incomplete evidence.` status alone is not enough. Without the job's input and exit-code record retained alongside it, the next person can only see the result's color and cannot tell whether the job actually ran what was intended. This requirement came from the evidence gap in this record, not from a redefinition of source-code behavior.

## Still Unresolved After Recovery

The temporary recovery allowed the on-call shift to proceed, but the record does not contain enough material to conclude why the discrepancy appeared in this maintenance window. The available material cannot distinguish between a mismatch between the plan and the actual input, deprecation-related signals left during execution, or a result-retention method that exposed an incomplete status to the people handling the window. These possibilities were not individually verified at the time. Nor does the record establish any single file as the point responsible.

The old record therefore retains the sequence of "recover first, then gather evidence." Any later reinvestigation should first obtain the corresponding version, environment, CI job, input, and exit-code record, then check them against the results observed during the window. Without those materials, this page can only establish that a discrepancy occurred and that the temporary recovery worked; it cannot supply the missing root cause.
